tone_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2014 [2005-2014]. Proto viet-muong (Proto-Vietic). Working document, 2005 version revised to 2014, released 2020 under CC BY-NC-SA. HAL halshs-02490370.
tone_statements.quote: Dans les langues tonales ou le système s'est pleinement développé (sous-groupes 7 et 8), il y a fréquemment confusion des tons a 4 et a 6 . … Les quatre parlers mường ont, comme le viet, un système de base à six tons parfois réduit à cinq. Dans les quatre parlers utilisés ici, Hòa Bình (HB), Sơn La (SL), Thanh Hóa (TH) et Mường Bi (MB), les anciennes liquides finales sont confondues et représentées respectivement par -ə, -l, -n et -l.
tone_statements.translation: In the tonal languages where the system has fully developed (subgroups 7 and 8), there is frequently merger of tones a4 and a6. … The four Muong dialects have, like Viet, a basic system of six tones sometimes reduced to five. In the four dialects used here, Hoa Binh (HB), Son La (SL), Thanh Hoa (TH) and Muong Bi (MB), the old final liquids are merged and represented respectively by -ə, -l, -n and -l.
tone_statements.locator: unnumbered introduction: 'Tonogenèse' and 'Caractéristiques phonétiques des langues/dialectes VM'
tone_statements.summary: Muong dialects (Hoa Binh, Son La, Thanh Hoa, Muong Bi) have, like Vietnamese, a basic six-tone system, sometimes five (a4 and a6 often merge); units given only as categories a1-a6, not characterised.

tone_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel (2004). The origin of tones in Viet-Muong. In Papers from the Eleventh Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 2001. Arizona State University Programme for Southeast Asian Studies Monograph Series Press. pp. 297--313.
tone_statements.quote: The relative chronology of these two major phenomena for each language led to different types of tone systems (Ferlus 1998a). + If the devoicing of plosive initials took place after the complete loss of the two laryngeal features -? and -h, then the language developed a six-tone basic system as in northern VM languages (Vietnamese, Mường, Thổ). * If the devoicing took place after the change of the laryngeal constriction -?, while final spirant =h was still preserved, then the language developed a four-tone basic system as in southern VM languages (Maleng, Arem, Sách/Rục, Thavung).
tone_statements.summary: Tonogenesis study: Muong, with Vietnamese and Tho, developed a 'six-tone basic system' (three old laryngeal rhyme types, each split by initial devoicing); Muong tone units not characterised.

tone_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1999. Les disharmonies tonales en viet-muong et leurs implications historiques. Cahiers de linguistique - Asie orientale 28(1): 83-100.
tone_statements.quote: Toutes les langues du groupe vietique sont des langues tonales. Le ton se manifeste sur la voyelle de la syllabe principale du mot … Le nombre des tons contrastifs peut aller de six (vietnamien, mường, cuối) à quatre (pong, sách/rục, thavung) … Le vietnamien, le mường et le cuối possèdent un système de base à 6 (+2) tons, six pour les syllabes en finale sonore et deux pour les syllabes en finale sourde (Ferlus 1998). Nous employons ici le système de notation étymologique par des numéros pour indiquer les catégories tonales, indépendamment des réalisations phonétiques.
tone_statements.translation: All the languages of the Vietic group are tone languages. Tone is realised on the vowel of the main syllable of the word … The number of contrastive tones ranges from six (Vietnamese, Muong, Cuoi) to four (Pong, Sach/Ruc, Thavung) … Vietnamese, Muong and Cuoi have a basic system of 6 (+2) tones, six for syllables with a sonorant final and two for syllables with a voiceless (stop) final (Ferlus 1998). We use here the etymological notation by numbers to indicate the tonal categories, independently of the phonetic realisations.
tone_statements.locator: HAL version p. 1, introduction before 'Premier type de disharmonie tonale', with the notation table (= CLAO 28(1) opening pages 83-84)
tone_statements.summary: Six contrastive tones a1-a6 in sonorant-final syllables plus two categories a7-a8 in stop-final syllables (6+2), in high and low series; etymological categories only, units not characterised.

tone_statements.quote: 2.3.4. ... Căn cứ vào hai tiêu chí đó, có thể phân xuất hệ thống thanh điệu M.Bi thành năm thanh ... Cả 5 thanh được phân bố cho âm tiết không đóng, còn âm tiết đóng chỉ nhận thanh 3 và thanh 5. ... 3.4. Số lượng thanh điệu của tất cả các thổ ngữ có sự thống nhất tuyệt đối. Chúng tôi gặp đầy đủ năm thanh ở bất kì thổ ngữ nào, không một thổ ngữ có dấu vết bốn thanh hoặc 6 thanh. Điều đó chứng tỏ thanh điệu tiếng Mường dường như đã hoàn thành quá trình biến đổi và đang ổn định.
tone_statements.translation: 2.3.4. ... On the basis of those two criteria [register and contour] the Mường Bi tone system can be analysed into five tones ... All 5 tones are distributed over non-closed syllables, whereas closed [stop-final] syllables take only tone 3 and tone 5. ... 3.4. The number of tones is absolutely uniform across all the local varieties. We find the full five tones in every variety; not one variety shows a trace of four tones or of 6 tones. This shows that the Muong tone system seems to have completed its process of change and is stable.

tone_statements.summary: Five tones (numbered 1-5) in Mường Bi and in every Muong variety surveyed; distinctive features per the p. 9 table: register high/low(-) = 1+,2-,3-,4+,5+; glottalized/broken ('gãy') = 2,4,5 vs 1,3 (-); rising = 2,3,4 vs falling = 1,5 (as read from the typewritten table). tone_statements.citation: Barker, Milton E. 1966. Vietnamese-Muong tone correspondences. In Norman H. Zide (ed.), Studies in Comparative Austroasiatic Linguistics (Indo-Iranian Monographs 5), 9-25. The Hague: Mouton.
tone_statements.quote: With the exception of certain compounds, reduplicative patterns, and loan words, Vietnamese and Muong are both monosyllabic languages with one phonemic tone occurring on each syllable (word). ... Muong has a system of five phonemic tones: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, and high-mid level. In words with a final stop (p, t, ch, c), this five-way contrast is neutralized to a two-way contrast, the two being phonetically high rising and high-mid level. ... [fn. 7] Words with high-mid level tone without a final stop (p, t, ch, c) have a final glottal stop as an integral part of the tone, whether there is another final consonant or not.
tone_statements.locator: p. 10 and footnote 7; correspondence table p. 11

tone_statements.summary: Five phonemic tones on the syllable: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, high-mid level (the last with final glottal stop in non-stop-final words); two-way contrast (high rising vs high-mid level) in stop-final syllables; correspondences VN ngang=M mid level, sắc(open)=low rising constricted, sắc(checked)=high rising checked, hỏi=high rising, huyền=low falling, ngã=high-m…

tone.summary: Five phonemic tones on the syllable: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, high-mid level (the last with final glottal stop in non-stop-final words); two-way contrast (high rising vs high-mid level) in stop-final syllables; correspondences VN ngang=M mid level, sắc(open)=low rising constricted, sắc(checked)=high rising checked, hỏi=high rising, huyền=low falling, ngã=high-m…
tone.says: Muong has five phonemic tones (mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, high-mid level), one tone per syllable; in stop-final syllables the contrast neutralizes to two (high rising, high-mid level); high-mid level tone carries a final glottal stop; then regular Vietnamese-Muong tone correspondences with cognate lists.

tone.quote: The relative chronology of these two major phenomena for each language led to different types of tone systems (Ferlus 1998a). + If the devoicing of plosive initials took place after the complete loss of the two laryngeal features -? and -h, then the language developed a six-tone basic system as in northern VM languages (Vietnamese, Mường, Thổ). * If the devoicing took place after the change of the laryngeal constriction -?, while final spirant =h was still preserved, then the language developed a four-tone basic system as in southern VM languages (Maleng, Arem, Sách/Rục, Thavung).
tone.summary: Tonogenesis study: Muong, with Vietnamese and Tho, developed a 'six-tone basic system' (three old laryngeal rhyme types, each split by initial devoicing); Muong tone units not characterised.
